title: Wiggle Sort II
description: Rearrange an array into an alternating less-than/greater-than pattern, using a sort-then-reverse-interleave strategy that safely handles duplicates.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given an integer array nums, reorder it in place so that nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] > ... (alternating strictly less-than, greater-than). The array may contain duplicate values; multiple valid arrangements can exist, so this document uses one specific deterministic algorithm and shows its exact output.

blocks.caption: Splitting the sorted array into a smaller half and larger half, then interleaving from each half's tail, produces a safe wiggle arrangement even with duplicates.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (can contain duplicate values)"],["Output","A rearrangement satisfying nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] > ..."],["Note","Any valid arrangement is accepted by the original problem; this document verifies one specific algorithm's deterministic result"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Sorting first, then splitting into a "smaller half" and "larger half," guarantees that any value from the larger half is strictly greater than any value from the smaller half (as long as there are no values straddling the split with ties handled carefully). Interleaving even positions from one half and odd positions from the other, in REVERSE order within each half, avoids placing two equal or adjacent-in-sorted-order values next to each other.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The reverse-interleave trick (filling from the END of each half rather than the start) is specifically what prevents duplicate values from ending up adjacent, which would violate the strict less-than/greater-than requirement.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a sorted deck of cards split into a weaker half and a stronger half. Seats alternate even and odd. Even seats are filled from the weaker half, strongest card of that half first; odd seats are filled from the stronger half, strongest card of that half first. Filling from the STRONGEST end of each half downward (rather than the weakest end upward) is what keeps duplicate values from landing next to each other.

blocks.caption: Filling from the strongest end of each half downward avoids placing duplicates adjacently.

items: Sort the array first, then split it into a smaller (lower) half and a larger (upper) half.
Fill EVEN positions (0, 2, 4, ...) with the smaller half, taken from its LARGEST value downward.
Fill ODD positions (1, 3, 5, ...) with the larger half, taken from its LARGEST value downward.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
nums = [1,5,1,1,6,4]. Sorted: [1,1,1,4,5,6]. n=6, mid=(6+1)/2=3 (integer division), so the smaller half is indices 0..2 ([1,1,1]) and the larger half is indices 3..5 ([4,5,6]).

blocks.text: The final arrangement is [1, 6, 1, 5, 1, 4], which satisfies 1<6>1<5>1<4, and matches a valid expected output for this exact input.
5. How Should We Think?

A direct split-and-interleave (filling each half from its SMALLEST end upward) works for arrays without duplicates, but can place two equal or adjacent values next to each other when duplicates are spread across the middle of the sorted array, violating the strict inequality requirement.

Filling from the LARGEST end of each half DOWNWARD instead spreads any duplicate values as far apart as possible in the final arrangement, since duplicates that were adjacent in sorted order end up on opposite "ends" of their half's fill order, landing far apart in the final interleaved result.
6. Brute Force Solution
Sort the array, then fill each half from its smallest end upward (a simpler interleave that works correctly when there are no problematic duplicate placements).
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n log n)","Sorting the array"],["Space","O(n)","The sorted copy and result array"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Filling each half from its smallest end can place two equal values from across the split adjacent to each other in some duplicate-heavy inputs, breaking the strict inequality requirement.
8. Optimize the Solution

Sort the array and split into a smaller half and larger half. Fill even positions from the smaller half's LARGEST value downward, and odd positions from the larger half's LARGEST value downward. This reverse-fill order keeps duplicate values maximally spread apart in the result, correctly handling inputs with repeated values.

items: Sort the array, O(n log n).
Split into a smaller half (first ceil(n/2) sorted values) and a larger half (the rest).
Fill even positions from the smaller half's tail backward, odd positions from the larger half's tail backward.

blocks.text: 9. Optimized Solution

codes.python:
def wiggle_sort(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    sorted_nums = sorted(nums)
    result = [0] * n

    mid = (n + 1) // 2
    j, k = mid - 1, n - 1
    for i in range(n):
        if i % 2 == 0:
            result[i] = sorted_nums[j]
            j -= 1
        else:
            result[i] = sorted_nums[k]
            k -= 1

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(wiggle_sort([1, 5, 1, 1, 6, 4]))
    print(wiggle_sort([1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1]))

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Both share the same asymptotic complexity; the reverse-fill version is the one that correctly handles duplicate-heavy inputs without violating the strict inequality requirement.
11. Key Takeaways

items: Splitting a sorted array into two halves and interleaving them is the standard wiggle-sort technique.
Filling from the LARGEST end of each half downward (not the smallest end upward) is what safely handles duplicate values without violating strict inequalities.
This reverse-fill trick generalizes to any "interleave two sorted groups while avoiding adjacency ties" rearrangement problem.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Wiggle Sort II is solved by sorting the array, splitting it into a smaller half and a larger half, and interleaving even positions from the smaller half and odd positions from the larger half, filling each half from its largest remaining value downward. This reverse-fill order safely handles duplicate values, giving a valid wiggle arrangement in O(n log n) time.
